claims.subject: e-lovelace-notes
claims.text: In 1843 Ada Lovelace published a paper on Charles Babbage's unbuilt Analytical Engine.

sources.note: Dates the Lovelace work on the Analytical Engine to 1843.
Says her 1843 paper about Babbage's unbuilt Analytical Engine holds the table of formulae sometimes called the first programme.
States that Lovelace published an account of the Analytical Engine in 1843.

claims.subject: e-eniac-announced
claims.text: ENIAC, the first general-purpose electronic computer, was announced to the public on 14 February 1946 and was front-page news in The New York Times the next day.

sources.note: Says ENIAC was originally announced on 14 February 1946 and calls it the first general-purpose electronic computer.
Says the New York Times announced the unveiling of the machine on 14 February 1946.
Puts the front-page New York Times story on 15 February 1946, one day later than the other two pages date the announcement.

claims.subject: e-transistor
claims.text: In December 1947 John Bardeen and Walter Brattain, working at Bell Telephone Laboratories, achieved transistor action in a germanium point-contact device.

sources.note: Names Bardeen and Brattain and gives December 1947 for transistor action in a germanium point-contact device.
Gives 17 November to 23 December 1947 at Bell Laboratories for the work of Brattain and Bardeen under Shockley.
Gives 1947 for the semiconductor amplifier of Bardeen and Brattain, later named the transistor; no month.

claims.subject: e-baby
claims.text: The Manchester Baby, the first stored-program electronic computer, ran its first program on 21 June 1948.

sources.note: Gives 21 June 1948 for the first program run by Baby, written by Kilburn.
Gives 21 June 1948 for the first successful program run of the machine built by Williams and Kilburn.
Gives 21 June 1948 for the first program to run on an electronic stored-program computer at Manchester.

claims.subject: e-arpanet-first
claims.text: On 29 October 1969 the first message was sent over the ARPANET, from UCLA to the Stanford Research Institute.

sources.note: Gives 10:30 p.m. on 29 October 1969 for the first ARPANET message, sent from UCLA to the Stanford Research Institute.
Records the first host-to-host connection, UCLA to SRI, on 29 October 1969.
Gives 10:30 p.m. on 29 October 1969 for the first transmission, when UCLA tried to send a message to SRI.

claims.subject: e-ibm-pc
claims.text: IBM unveiled its Personal Computer, the IBM PC, on 12 August 1981 in New York.

sources.note: Gives 12 August 1981 for the unveiling of the IBM PC at a New York hotel; the only one of the three that gives the day.
Lists the introduction of IBM's Personal Computer under 1981; no day.
Says IBM introduced its PC in 1981; no day.

claims.subject: e-tcpip-switch
claims.text: The ARPANET changed over from the NCP protocol to TCP/IP on 1 January 1983.

sources.note: Describes the changeover of the ARPANET host protocol from NCP to TCP/IP as of 1 January 1983, in a single flag-day.
The 1981 plan for the changeover; it sets 1 January 1983 as the date for a complete switch from NCP to TCP.
Says the ARPANET standardised on TCP/IP in January 1983.

claims.subject: e-web-proposal
claims.text: In March 1989 Tim Berners-Lee wrote and circulated at CERN the proposal "Information Management: A Proposal", the first proposal for what became the World Wide Web.

sources.note: Holds the proposal itself, written by Tim Berners-Lee at CERN in March 1989 and recirculated in May 1990.
Lists the first project proposal, written and circulated for comment, in March 1989.
Dates the writing and circulation of the proposal at CERN to March 1989.
